newsitem.title: CANADA: Winnipeg rattled as flood crest bursts through dike.
newsitem.headline: Winnipeg rattled as flood crest bursts through dike.

text.p: One hundred Winnipeggers fled their apartment building on Thursday as cresting Red River flood waters burst through a sandbag dike.
"It became a difficulty early in the day when the basement flooded and then we evacuated about 100 people by midafternoon," Winnipeg Emergency Management spokesman Randy Hull said.
No one was injured in the dike breach at the south Winnipeg apartment block, Hull added.
The news rattled an already tense city of 650,000 people as the surging Red River neared its crest and emergency workers hoped other dikes could withstand the rising flood waters.

"People are on edge now. You see it creeping higher and higher every day coming to work on the bus," Tammy Usipiuk said as she and co-workers returned from viewing water levels at the forks of the Red and Assiniboine Rivers.
The forks are at the centre of Winnipeg, Manitoba's capital and biggest city.
About 29,000 Canadians and 50,000 Americans have been displaced and four Canadians have died so far in the most extensive Red River flooding since 1852.

"We've dealt with river levels five feet (1.5 metres) lower. Once you're above that you're in unknown territory and while we're above that comfort level, we're going to be uncomfortable," Winnipeg City Commissioner Bill Carroll said.

About 8,800 Winnipeggers have had to flee their homes as the rising river seeped through dikes shielding five city streets on Wednesday and inundated Canadian farmland covering an area twice the size of Hong Kong. Those dikes were repaired and five military rapid response teams were deployed across the city.

"We will deploy all the resources necessary," Canadian Defence Minister Doug Young told a news briefing. Some 7,900 soldiers will be deployed across Manitoba by Sunday, one day before the western edge of the Red River crests at a weak point in the city's defences.
Manitoba's capital is protected by a 25-mile (40-km) dike southwest of the city that was completed on Wednesday.
"It's very surreal to see this mountain of rock rising on the horizon," evacuated area farmer Ray Kabernick said. "We feel really confident being on the side of the dike that we're on."
But authorities wee worried the hastily built dike may break under the pressure of the river, which has flooded 800 square miles (2,100 sq km) of Manitoba land.

"We're in a good, solid holding pattern today," Winnipeg Mayor Susan Thompson said as the Red River rose to within an inch (2.5 cm) of its forecast peak downtown. "But the crest is not a one-day event. The peak will be with us for a week and then will recede slowly."

If the southwest dike breached, engineers said Red River headwaters might reach Winnipeg within six hours and could raise the river's crest another two feet (60 cm) above its forecast peak downtown within 40 hours.
But emergency officials said they would divert those waters into a 29-mile (47-km) ditch parting the rising "Red Sea."
The white-capping flood waters overwhelmed the U.S. cities of Grand Forks and East Grand Forks in North Dakota and swallowed the Canadian town of Ste. Agathe and many farmsteads.

"It's just discouraging when people spent countless hours putting up sand dikes and it doesn't work," Morris area reeve, or mayor, Herm Martens said. "We're cautiously optimistic we're seeing the light at the end of the tunnel."
The Canadian government advanced C$25 million ($18 million) in disaster funds on Thursday in what Manitoba Premier Gary Filmon called the "largest civil disaster this century."
